endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers

endorsements.title: Texas SB 1188 (89th Legislature), electronic health records and AI disclosure
endorsements.quote: the practitioner reviews all records created with artificial intelligence in a manner that is consistent with medical records standards developed by the Texas Medical Board.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: AI t ools or systems cannot augment, create, or otherwise generate records, communications, or other content on behalf of a physician without that physician’s consent and final review.

endorsements.quote: This report is released to the patient and ordering clinician upon signing.

endorsements.quote: Although useful in these contexts, it is necessary for clinicians to critically review and validate any computer-generated text before it is used in any clinical setting or research.

endorsements.title: Automation and artificial intelligence in radiation therapy treatment planning
endorsements.quote: This will rely on clinician oversight to ‘approve’ the contours and provide feedback to vendors on model performance, 16 with an increased use of multimodal imaging.

endorsements.title: Generative Language Models and Open Notes: Exploring the Promise and Limitations
endorsements.quote: In this scenario, LLMs might offer initial draft documentation, which, crucially, should be supervised, and edited by clinicians whose key role in documentation will be to keep a check and balance on the current limitations with these models.

endorsements.issuer: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open

endorsements.title: An AI-Enabled Nursing Future With no Documentation Burden: A Vision for a New Reality

endorsements.title: Ambient technology in epilepsy clinical practice
endorsements.quote: Thus, it is crucial that a “human‐in‐the‐loop” (HITL) model is utilized to guard against inaccurate documentation, 35 which can lead to incorrect or even harmful treatment and paradoxically, decreased efficiency of chart review.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing machine-assisted translation in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Reinforce a translator-in-the-loop model that emphasizes LLM outputs should be a first draft with the final review remaining the translator’s responsibility

endorsements.title: Beyond Chatbots: Moving Toward Multistep Modular AI Agents in Medical Education
endorsements.quote: Every stage of the agentic pipeline therefore includes a mandatory checkpoint where educators review, revise, and approve an agent’s output before it is handed to the next specialist agent.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Drafting of Chest X-Ray Reports: 2025 Position Statement From the Korean Society of Thoracic Radiology Based on an Expert Survey
endorsements.quote: Therefore, AI drafts should serve only as preliminary reports, awaiting radiologist confirmation.

endorsements.title: Bridging the patient gap: exploring generative AI to support meaningful patient involvement in health technology assessment
endorsements.quote: Equally important is human oversight: validation by patient representatives, HTA staff or independent reviewers is indispensable to guarantee accuracy and contextual nuance.

endorsements.title: The Clinician as DIRECTOR: Operationalizing Cinematic Storytelling for Clinical Documentation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
endorsements.quote: Health systems can operationalize this approach by requiring clinician-authored narrative anchors before note finalization.

endorsements.title: AI Scribe Use in Residency Training: A Call for Specialty Society Guidance in Graduate Medical Education
endorsements.issuer: Advances in medical education and practice
endorsements.quote: Such policies should incorporate mandatory resident review and note sign-off of AI-generated notes, clear accountability protocols, patient consent standards, and limitations on use depending on the note section such as formulation of assessment and plan.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence documentation in trauma resuscitation: efficiency requires guardrails
endorsements.quote: Draft documentation generated by AI systems must be subject to mandatory human review of high-risk elements, including primary survey findings, neurologic status, anticoagulation history, procedures performed, and disposition decisions.

endorsements.title: Barriers and opportunities of scaling ambient AI scribes for clinical documentation across diverse healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: Hence, institutions must define accountability structures and ensure clinicians carefully review the generated text.

endorsements.title: Navigating the artificial intelligence landscape in trauma, critical care and emergency general surgery: insights from the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) 2025 Annual Meeting Panel Discussion
endorsements.quote: However, because they remain susceptible to errors and hallucinations, 12 their outputs require systematic review, and their deployment should be governed by clear validation and oversight processes.

endorsements.title: Ethical-Regulatory Guidelines for AI in Palliative Care Rehabilitation
endorsements.quote: AI-supported rehabilitation recommendations should be reviewed and validated by qualified healthcare professionals; roles and responsibilities for AI use should be clearly defined; AI outputs and clinician decisions should be documented in the clinical record.

endorsements.title: Governing Generative AI in Healthcare: A Normative Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Authority, Trust, and the Architecture of Responsibility
endorsements.quote: At Tier 1, the LLM produces a draft or summary—for example, a referral letter assembled from the patient’s record—which needs clinician review before being sent.

endorsements.title: Self-regulating the use of large language models in clinical practice: a risk-stratified approach
endorsements.quote: Governance actions include mandatory clinician review and confirmation before outputs are used in care.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Intensive Care: From Algorithmic Fluency to Clinical Accountability
endorsements.issuer: Indian journal of critical care medicine : peer-reviewed, official publication of Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine
endorsements.quote: Documentation review: Carefully check AI-assisted notes for inaccuracies.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Clinical Co-Pilot in Reminiscence Therapy: A Nurse-Led Model for Super-Aged Societies
endorsements.quote: no patient-facing content is delivered without nurse approval.

endorsements.title: Text-to-Video Generative Artificial Intelligence in Pediatrics: Potential Applications, Ethical Considerations, and Future Directions
endorsements.quote: A clear human‐in‐the‐loop review process is required, with responsibility assigned for clinical accuracy, updates, and incident response (e.g., correction of detected misinformation).

endorsements.title: An Evidence-Based Framework for Patient-Facing Artificial Intelligence Integration in the Emergency Department
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
endorsements.quote: The safest model is human-in-the-loop: generative AI drafts patient instructions, and clinicians review, edit, and contextualize content before release.

endorsements.title: A Human-Governed Clinical Informatics Framework for Safe AI-Assisted Mental Health Counseling: Secondary Framework Development and Requirement Mapping Study
endorsements.quote: A clinician must then approve, edit, reject, or request additional assessment, and only human-approved content may proceed to record integration and postdeployment monitoring.

endorsements.title: Using ambient AI in clinical consultations: reframing policy around clinical audit and patient safety
endorsements.quote: It stressed, however, that the evidence remains heterogeneous and that clinician oversight of AI-generated notes is essential ( 16 ).

endorsements.title: Reclaiming the Human Connection in Clinical Care With AI
endorsements.quote: Finally, clinicians must continue to maintain accountability for documentation accuracy and completeness, which entails reviewing, approving, and signing off on AI-drafted notes before they become part of the medical record.

endorsements.title: The Promise of Ambient AI Technology in Medical Education: Opportunities and Guardrails
endorsements.quote: Use an institutional attestation policy requiring explicit review of AI drafts, an audit trail of edits, faculty cosignature for any trainee-associated AI-drafted content, and education on accountability and liability.

endorsements.title: Governing medical AI under the EU AI Act: an integrated compliance-by-design framework
endorsements.quote: Configuration A requires clinician review before AI-generated content enters the medical record; Configuration B requires escalation procedures, uncertainty handling, and disclosure to patients that they are interacting with an AI system.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Should Not Prescribe Alone: A Risk-Stratified Pharmacy Governance Framework for Agentic Clinical Systems
endorsements.quote: Functions involving treatment initiation, dose adjustment, antimicrobial selection, therapeutic substitution or deprescribing require stronger evidence and mandatory pharmacist and prescriber validation [ 9 ].

evidence.title: Utilizing AI-Generated Plain Language Summaries to Enhance Interdisciplinary Understanding of Ophthalmology Notes: A Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Error rate in LLM-generated summaries after ophthalmologist review and editing, and on independent over-read
evidence.effect: Error rate was 26% on initial ophthalmologist review and editing and 15% on independent over-read of edited PLSs; 84.9% of errors were low risk and 0% carried risk of severe harm or death.
evidence.quote: PLS error rate on initial ophthalmologist review and editing was 26%, and 15% on independent ophthalmologist over-read of edited PLSs.

evidence.title: Provision of Radiology Reports Simplified With Large Language Models to Patients With Cancer: Impact on Patient Satisfaction
evidence.outcome: Radiologist review catching errors in LLM-simplified reports before release
evidence.effect: Radiologist supervision identified 3 of 50 simplified reports requiring corrections before provision to patients.
evidence.quote: Only three (of 50) simplified reports required corrections by the radiologist.

evidence.title: Evaluation of AI Summaries on Interdisciplinary Understanding of Ophthalmology Notes
evidence.outcome: Errors in LLM plain language summaries identified on ophthalmologist review and their risk of harm
evidence.effect: PLS error rate on ophthalmologist review was 26% (126 of 489); 83.9% (104 of 126) of errors low risk for harm, none severe harm or death; errors persisted despite physician review.
evidence.quote: PLS error rate on ophthalmologist review was 26% (126 of 489).
evidence.sample_unit: ophthalmologist review responses on LLM-generated plain language summaries (plus 362 nonophthalmology respondents preferring PLS)

evidence.title: Ambient AI Scribes to Create Educational Feedback Notes for Medical Students: Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Whether instructor editing of AI-drafted feedback notes corrected AI errors
evidence.effect: Most errors in AI summaries (6.8% mischaracterization, 1.7% hallucination) were corrected during instructor editing before submission.
evidence.quote: Review of 117 AI-generated feedback elements showed a 6.8% (n=8) mischaracterization and 1.7% (n=2) hallucination rate, with most errors corrected during editing.

evidence.title: Clinical Implementation of an Artificial Intelligence Algorithm for Magnetic Resonance-Derived Measurement of Total Kidney Volume
evidence.outcome: Difference between AI segmentation and radiologist/technologist-edited segmentation in TKV after clinician review
evidence.effect: Of 170 reviewed cases, 84 were manually edited; AI TKV output showed a small mean volume difference of -3.3% versus edited; disease class differed in five cases.
evidence.quote: Of manually edited cases (n=84), the AI-algorithm TKV output showed a small mean volume difference of -3.3%.

evidence.title: AI-Human Hybrid Workflow Enhances Teleophthalmology for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.outcome: Accuracy after retina specialist overread of AI-positive results before referral
evidence.effect: AI alone: sensitivity 95.5%, specificity 60.3%, PPV 47.7%; with specialist overread of MTMDR-positive results: PPV 95.5%, accuracy 97.4%, sensitivity 95.5%, specificity 98.2%. Overread of AI-ungradable raised gradability from 63.5% to 95.6%.
evidence.quote: Under this 2-step workflow, the positive predictive value increased to 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%–100%), along with accuracy of 97.4%, sensitivity of 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%–100%), and specificity of 98.2% (95% CI, 94.6%–100%) ( Figs 6 , 15 ).

evidence.title: Real-world performance evaluation of commercial autocontouring software for head and neck cancer radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Differences between AI-generated contours and clinician-reviewed final contours, geometric and dosimetric
evidence.effect: Dosimetric comparison of AI-contours versus final reviewed contours showed clinically significant dose differences for larynx and elective nodal volumes, so clinician review altered contours; authors conclude final clinician review remains essential.
evidence.quote: Dosimetric evaluation demonstrated clinically significant dose differences for larynx and elective nodal volumes.

evidence.title: Deep learning-based Wilms tumor segmentation to create 3D models for surgical planning: Implementation in the clinical workflow
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician review and correction catches errors in AI segmentations
evidence.effect: 8/10 automated segmentations required correction, median correction time 11 min; errors included tumor border under-segmentation (n=3) and tumor/kidney border misidentification (n=3).
evidence.quote: In 8/10 patients the automated segmentation needed corrections (with a median correction time of 11 min).

evidence.title: Implementation outcomes of AI documentation support in routine clinical practice: A non-randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Documentation quality via senior physician review of AI-assisted discharge letters (revision counts)
evidence.effect: Revision frequency decreased within intervention group (1.36 ± 0.14 to 1.26 ± 0.08 per document); no significant interaction for revision count, so standards were maintained under supervision.
evidence.quote: This real-world evaluation suggests that AI documentation assistance is associated with improved documentation efficiency under routine clinical conditions, while maintaining documentation standards under established supervision processes.

evidence.title: Experience of Implementing Deep Learning-Based Automatic Contouring in Breast Radiation Therapy Planning: Insights From Over 2000 Cases
evidence.venue: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
evidence.outcome: Extent to which clinician review and revision changed AI auto-contours
evidence.effect: Reviewers revised auto-contours (final contours generally larger, more slices), but agreement between auto and final contours rose postimplementation, and lung segmentation was inaccurate. Analyzed 22,215 structures.
evidence.quote: The final contours were generally larger, encompassing more slices in the superior or inferior directions.

evidence.title: The Impact of a Neuroradiologist on the Report of a Real-World CT Perfusion Imaging Map Derived from Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning-Driven Software
evidence.outcome: Proportion of AI-derived CTP maps reportable before vs after neuroradiologist review
evidence.effect: AI CTP maps reportable in 65.2% of cases without artifacts; improved to 87.9% reportable after neuroradiologist review and correction
evidence.quote: The study found that CTP maps derived from AI software were reportable in 65.2% of cases without artifacts and improved to 87.9% reportable cases when reviewed by neuroradiologists.

evidence.title: Enhancing Patient Understanding of Radiology Reports Through Large Language Model-Generated Summaries, Clickable Terms, and Artificial Intelligence Videos
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Extent of clinician edits required to LLM-generated radiology report summaries before release
evidence.effect: Summaries required manual clinician edits: average 24.75 words removed, 0.13 words added per summary; lexical similarity 84.63%, semantic similarity 98.25%.
evidence.quote: However, LLM-summaries required manual clinician edits (average per summary: 24.75 words removed; 0.13 words added, lexical similarity = 84.63%; semantic similarity = 98.25%).

evidence.title: Evaluating an LLM-Assisted Workflow for Clinical Documentation:  A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial on Time and Quality
evidence.outcome: Document quality and creation time: clinician review/editing of LLM drafts vs clinician-only vs unedited LLM drafts
evidence.effect: Clinician-in-the-loop outperformed clinician-only in most quality domains; LLM-only drafts fastest but lowest quality. Summaries faster (β = −59.4 s, P = .047); referrals slower (β = 94.8 s, P<.001).
evidence.quote: LLM-only drafts were fastest but had the lowest quality.

evidence.title: Language-dependent diagnostic safety of medical AI systems: a cross-lingual benchmarking and prospective clinical study
evidence.outcome: physician edits to AI records
evidence.effect: 98·7% of records required physician edits; overall modification score 53·6%; Thai-pivot burden 59·0% vs English-pivot 5 0·7%, p=0·003.
evidence.quote: In the prospective study, 98·7% of records required physician edits (overall modification score 53·6%); Thai-pivot correction burden (59·0%) exceeded English-pivot (5 0·7%, p=0·003) and Chinese-direct (51·0%, p=0·004).

evidence.title: Quality, consistency, and clinical safety of AI-generated versus clinician-written clinical notes: a multi-country paired simulation study
evidence.outcome: Fraction of documentation errors identified by unaided clinician review versus calibrated automated reviewer
evidence.effect: Unaided clinician review identified roughly 12% of the errors the calibrated reviewer retained, and a smaller fraction in AI notes than in clinician notes.
evidence.quote: Unaided clinician review identified roughly 12% of the errors the calibrated reviewer retained, and a smaller fraction in AI notes than in clinician notes.
evidence.country: United Kingdom, Spain, Italy, France, Germany

evidence.title: Consensus, dissensus and synergy between clinicians and specialist foundation models in radiology report generation
evidence.outcome: report quality in clinician-AI collaborative composition
evidence.effect: synergistic improvement across all clinical settings for reports that contain errors
evidence.quote: For reports that contain errors we develop an assistive setting, the first demonstration of clinician-AI collaboration for radiology report composition, and we observe a synergistic improvement across all clinical settings.
evidence.sample_unit: certified radiologists evaluating AI-generated and human-written chest radiograph reports

evidence.title: Multimodal Generative Artificial Intelligence Model for Creating Radiology Reports for Chest Radiographs in Patients Undergoing Tuberculosis Screening
evidence.outcome: Radiologist acceptance of AI-generated reports without modification, by normal/abnormal status
evidence.effect: Reader 1 accepted 91.7% of normal and 52.4% of abnormal reports; reader 2 accepted 83.2% and 37.0%, showing many abnormal reports needed modification.
evidence.quote: Among normal and abnormal radiographs, reader 1 accepted 91.7% and 52.4%, whereas reader 2 accepted 83.2% and 37.0%, respectively, of AI-generated reports.
evidence.country: Unknown (public datasets from tuberculosis screening programs)

evidence.title: Understanding Clinician Perceptions of GenAI: A Mixed Methods Analysis of Clinical Documentation Tasks
evidence.outcome: perceived safety of documentation automation
evidence.effect: Low automation was safe/caution for >70%; high automation was probably/definitely unsafe for 30-35% across tasks.
evidence.quote: Notably, while low automation was consistently rated as “Safe” or “Safe with Caution” by over 70% of participants, high automation received “Probably Unsafe” or “Definitely Unsafe” ratings from 30-35% of participants across tasks (Figs. 4 and 5 ).

evidence.title: Surgeon, Trainee, or GPT? A Blinded Multicentric Study of AI-Augmented Operative Notes
evidence.outcome: Approval rate of operative notes: GPT-only versus attending-edited hybrid (attending plus GPT)
evidence.effect: Hybrid attending+GPT notes had the highest 'as is' approval rate (79%), versus 23% for GPT-only notes, which had the most omissions and overdocumentation.
evidence.quote: Hybrid notes written by an attending surgeon with GPT assistance received the highest average domain scores and the highest "as is" approval rate (79%), outperforming all other groups.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Accuracy and Efficiency of AI-Generated Radiology Reports Based on Positive Findings-A Qualitative Assessment of AI in Radiology
evidence.outcome: Whether radiologist review corrects errors in AI-drafted reports
evidence.effect: Minor formatting errors and occasional anatomical misinterpretations in AI reports were easily corrected by the radiologist during review; accuracy rated 4.65 vs 3.81 with dictation (p<0.0001).
evidence.quote: Minor formatting errors and occasional anatomical misinterpretations were observed in AI-generated reports, but could be easily corrected by the radiologist during review.
evidence.sample_unit: imaging cases (MRI knee, MRI lumbar spine, CT head, CT abdomen/pelvis)

evidence.title: Better understanding: can a large language model safely improve readability of patient information leaflets in interventional radiology?
evidence.outcome: Factual accuracy of LLM-modified leaflets as rated by consultant radiologists
evidence.effect: Most LLM-modified PILs had minor factual accuracy concerns identified by three consultant radiologists; no errors that could cause serious patient harm detected.
evidence.quote: Human evaluation revealed that most LLM-modified PILs had minor concerns regarding factual accuracy, but no errors that could result in serious patient harm were detected.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Assistant for Emergency Department Discharge Documentation
evidence.outcome: Whether physician review of LLM drafts removed the confabulation before finalizing notes
evidence.effect: The single confabulation in 50 LLM drafts was removed in 5 of 6 LLM-assisted notes; the least-experienced physician missed it. Physician editing improved conciseness but slightly lowered completeness and correctness scores versus drafts.
evidence.quote: The single confabulation documented unperformed procedures (splint application, dressing) and was removed in 5 of 6 LLM-assisted notes—by all except the least-experienced physician—indicating that brief clinician review remains necessary despite high baseline quality.

evidence.title: Generating subjective, objective, assessment, and plan (SOAP)-structured medication logs using DeepSeek-R1 through prompt engineering and multi-source clinical information
evidence.outcome: Whether pharmacist review of AI-generated logs identifies and corrects errors
evidence.effect: Pharmacist review identified recurrent errors and corrected them, with BERT F1 rising from 0.68 to 0.71 (P<0.05), showing review was essential.
evidence.quote: Therefore, the review of DeepSeek-R1-generated texts by clinical pharmacists is indispensable.

evidence.title: A prospective multicenter trial of deep learning auto-segmentation for organs at risk in thoracic radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of physician-revised AI contours vs unrevised AI contours
evidence.effect: AI-assisted (physician-revised) contours significantly more accurate than AI-only for 6 of 11 OARs (54.5%); revision eliminated EC-related trachea accuracy drop.
evidence.quote: AI-assisted delineation also achieved significantly higher accuracy than AI delineation for 6 out of 11 OARs (54.5%): the heart, aorta, liver, trachea, spinal cord, and esophagus (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
evidence.outcome: Content quality (risk, overall) of LLM-simplified consent forms with vs without clinician revision
evidence.effect: Clinician revision raised risk score from 3.28 to 3.69 (p=0.016) and overall from 2.86 to 3.64 (p=0.004); LMM risk β=0.42, overall β=0.78; restored to original-level quality.
evidence.quote: The risk score increased from 3.28 (SD = 0.55) to 3.69 (SD = 0.66), p = 0.016; the overall score also rose from 2.86 (SD = 0.36) to 3.64 (SD = 0.31), p = 0.004.
evidence.sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

evidence.title: A hybrid large language model framework for structured data entry from code-switched persian clinical speech
evidence.outcome: Incorrectly filled fields after human review
evidence.effect: Hybrid review reduced IFF from 10% to 3% in medium forms and by 5 percentage points in large forms.
evidence.quote: The hybrid configuration consistently improves suggestion correctness, while the most substantial error mitigation is observed in the Incorrectly Filled Fields Percentage, which declines markedly–from 10% to 3% in medium forms and by 5 percentage points in large forms.

evidence.title: Performance of the Techcyte AI-based image analysis system for coproparasitological diagnosis in clinical stool specimens: a retrospective evaluation study
evidence.outcome: negative specimen identification before versus after operator review
evidence.effect: Correctly identified negative specimens increased from 2/31 initially to 29/31 after operator review due to discarding artifacts.
evidence.quote: This configuration explains the low number of correctly identified negative specimens (2/31) initially, and the high proportion of correctly identified negative specimens after operator review (29/31).

evidence.title: Clinician-supervised large language AI model after-discharge instruction generation for common emergency department presentations
evidence.outcome: clinical accuracy and readability
evidence.effect: Physician edits improved accuracy but paradoxically reduced objective readability scores.
evidence.quote: Physician edits improved accuracy but paradoxically reduced objective readability scores.

evidence.title: A large language models-assisted and expert-corrected workflow for preoperative anesthesia assessment drafts: A single-centre exploratory feasibility study
evidence.outcome: Whether expert review of LLM drafts identifies errors requiring correction before resident-facing use
evidence.effect: Expert review found 32 error instances across 15 cases; authors conclude expert correction was essential before resident-facing use.
evidence.quote: In this single-centre exploratory study, an LLM-assisted workflow was feasible for producing preliminary preoperative anesthesia assessment drafts, but expert correction was essential before resident-facing use.

evidence.title: Perceptions and Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence Among Physical Therapy Professionals in Ohio: A Cross-Sectional Survey
evidence.outcome: Self-reported editing of AI-generated content before professional use
evidence.effect: 91.7% of PT users and 96.0% of PTA users reported editing AI-generated content before professional use.
evidence.quote: Nearly all users reported editing AI-generated content before professional use (PTs: 91.7%; PTAs: 96.0%), and over 97% of both groups had never entered personally identifiable information into AI systems.

evidence.title: MedAgentBrief for Hospital Course Summarization: Safety, Use, and Discharge Documentation Burden
evidence.outcome: Errors (omissions, inaccuracies, hallucinations) and potential harm in unedited AI-drafted hospital course summaries
evidence.effect: Feedback on 100 summaries noted omissions (25%), inaccuracies (20%), hallucinations (2%). 88% of unedited summaries had no harm potential, 1% likely moderate harm, no severe harm reported.
evidence.quote: Feedback on 100 summaries (40.2%) noted omissions (25%) and inaccuracies (20%) but rare hallucinations (2%).

evidence.title: From Conversation to Chart: An Analysis of Clinician Edits to Ambient AI Draft Notes
evidence.outcome: Proportion of ambient AI draft notes edited by clinicians before signing
evidence.effect: 84.4% of 23,760 notes were edited before sign-off, so about 15.6% were signed unedited; edit rates varied by note section, specialty and individual clinician.
evidence.quote: Across 23,760 notes that included one or more ambient AI sections, 84.4% were edited by clinicians before signing off.

evidence.title: Quality of Clinical Notes Created by Ambient Listening Generative AI: Pragmatic Prospective Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Errors in AI drafted notes with potential for serious harm if not corrected
evidence.effect: 19 (5.3%) notes contained errors rated serious or imminent risk (severity 4-5); 14.9% (143/960) of notes left entirely unedited.
evidence.quote: However, because a small number contained errors that carried the risk of serious harm if not corrected, careful clinician review of notes remains imperative.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated clinic notes evaluated by physicians

evidence.title: Physician-Reported Safety Outcomes of AI-Generated Hospital Course Summaries
evidence.outcome: Errors (omissions, inaccuracies, hallucinations) and physician-rated harm potential in unedited AI hospital course summaries
evidence.effect: Among 100 summaries with feedback: omissions 25%, inaccuracies 20%, hallucinations 2%. Unedited summaries: 88 (88.0%) no harm potential, 1 (1.0%) likely moderate harm, no severe harm.
evidence.quote: Feedback on 100 summaries (88 of 219 used summaries [40.2%] and 12 of 165 unused summaries [7.3%]) noted omissions (25 summaries [25.0%]) and inaccuracies (20 summaries [20.0%]) but rare hallucinations (2 summaries [2.0%]).

evidence.title: Language-dependent diagnostic safety of medical AI systems: a cross-lingual benchmarking and prospective clinical study
evidence.outcome: Proportion of AI-generated records needing physician edits in prospective study
evidence.effect: 98.7% of records required physician edits; overall modification score 53.6%.
evidence.quote: In the prospective study, 98·7% of records required physician edits (overall modification score 53·6%); Thai-pivot correction burden (59·0%) exceeded English-pivot (5 0·7%, p=0·003) and Chinese-direct (51·0%, p=0·004).

evidence.title: Clinical safety evaluation of ambient voice technologies in surgical documentation
evidence.outcome: Clinically significant errors in AI-transcribed clinical documentation, including severe harm potential
evidence.effect: Errors with potential for severe harm or death (NHS Levels 3-4) totalled n=35, concentrated in medication type and dose (37.1%) and investigations/lab results (34.3%).
evidence.quote: Errors with potential to cause severe harm or death (NHS England Levels 3-4) totalled n=35 across systems and were concentrated in medication type and dose (37.1%) and investigations and laboratory results (34.3%).

evidence.title: First the Rules, Then the Summary: Piloting a Design for Accurate LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
evidence.outcome: Narrative summary hard and soft errors
evidence.effect: No hard errors; soft errors in 8 of 25 briefs (32%).
evidence.quote: Two raters independently coded the narrative prose and found no hard errors (factual contradictions of the data) and soft errors in 8 of 25 briefs (32%), where information was combined across waves or measures, which the harness does not check.

evidence.title: Clinical Evaluation of a Novel Deep Learning-Based Auto-Segmentation Software: Utility and Potential Pitfalls
evidence.outcome: Clinical acceptability of AI auto-contours on visual review, and accuracy versus expert manual contours
evidence.effect: Mean DSC 0.79 ± 0.19, HD95 6.35 ± 12.2 mm; 93.5% (315/337) of contours acceptable, so about 6.5% failed; lower performance in small and low-contrast structures and atypical cases.
evidence.quote: However, performance variability in atypical cases underscores the necessity of rigorous visual verification by experts for clinical implementation.

evidence.title: Does a Safety-Priming Instruction Reduce Risk-Fact Omission in Psychiatric Note Summarization? A Synthetic-Vignette Study of Small Open-Weight Language Models
evidence.outcome: risk-fact omission in psychiatric note summarization
evidence.effect: baseline risk-fact omission ranged from 4% to 26% across four models, with suicidality omitted in up to 50% of cases for weaker models
evidence.quote: Baseline (generic-instruction) risk-fact omission ranges from 4% to 26% across the four models the smallest model omits the safety-critical fact roughly one time in four.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic psychiatric intake vignettes per condition

evidence.title: Physician- and Large Language Model-Generated Hospital Discharge Summaries: A Blinded, Comparative Quality and Safety Study
evidence.outcome: Errors (inaccuracies, omissions, hallucinations) and potential harm in LLM-drafted discharge summaries
evidence.effect: LLM narratives averaged 2.91 errors per summary vs 1.82 for physicians; overall potential harm 0.84 vs 0.36 (p<0.001), though low (<1 on 0-7 scale).
evidence.quote: LLM-generated narratives contained more unique errors (average 2.91 [SD 2.54] errors per summary) than physician-generated narratives (1.82 [SD 1.94]).
evidence.sample_unit: inpatient hospital medicine encounters (discharge summary narratives)

evidence.title: ChatGPT makes medicine easy to swallow: an exploratory case study on simplified radiology reports
evidence.outcome: Radiologist ratings of factual correctness, completeness, and potential harm of ChatGPT-simplified reports
evidence.effect: Most radiologists agreed simplified reports were correct, complete, and not harmful, but some raters reported incorrect statements, missed relevant medical information, and potentially harmful passages.
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, instances of incorrect statements, missed relevant medical information, and potentially harmful passages were reported.
evidence.sample_unit: radiologists rating three fictitious simplified radiology reports

evidence.title: ChatGPT's Ability to Assist with Clinical Documentation: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.outcome: Proportion of ChatGPT-generated HPI documents containing erroneous information
evidence.effect: ChatGPT included erroneous information in 36% of documents; ChatGPT documents were longer and had higher PDQI quality scores than dictation and typing.

commentary.bottom_line: Clinician review changed AI drafts and caught some errors before release across notes, reports, and image contours, but in one trial 15% of summaries still contained errors after editing and over-read, and in one simulation unaided reviewers found about 12% of errors. The studies suggest that review is necessary, while its reliability as a standalone safeguard remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Four randomized trials and several comparator studies report that review changed AI outputs. Most compare the same draft before and after editing rather than randomizing review itself. Outcomes are error counts or quality scores, not patient harm, and many studies test image contours or teaching feedback. These limits in directness and design suggest low certainty.

Review catches some errors but misses others. In one trial, 26% of plain language summaries had errors on ophthalmologist review and 15% on independent over-read after editing, though none carried severe harm risk. In a simulation, unaided clinicians found about 12% of errors. In one deployment, 5.3% of drafts had serious-risk errors and 14.9% of notes went unedited.

Review effort varies by task. Clinicians corrected 8 of 10 kidney tumor segmentations, with a median correction time of 11 minutes. In a Japanese trial, reviewing drafts shortened summary writing by 59.4 seconds but lengthened referral letters by 94.8 seconds. Among 23,760 ambient notes, edit rates differed by section, specialty, and clinician, which may reflect uneven review fidelity.

Four tests involved non-English documentation and one involved low-literacy leaflets, all in offline or simulated settings. Physician edit burden was 59.0% for Thai-pivot records versus 50.7% for English-pivot records, which suggests review demands may rise for non-English encounters. Clinician revision restored the quality of simplified Chinese consent forms. No test included Medicaid or safety-net settings.

Texas SB 1188 requires practitioners to review all AI-created records, and professional guidance calls for physician approval. No study tests whether such mandates change error rates. Deployment data show that 14.9% and 15.6% of AI notes were signed without edits. This suggests that a signature alone may not document meaningful review, which bears on how compliance is audited.

Review burden may concentrate on abnormal findings. Radiologists accepted 91.7% and 83.2% of AI reports on normal chest films without changes, compared with 52.4% and 37.0% on abnormal films. In a German deployment covering 15,615 discharge letters, senior physician revision counts held at about 1.3 per document, which suggests existing supervision structures may absorb AI drafts.

Radiologist review found that 3 of 50 simplified reports needed correction before patients received them. When five urologists reviewed AI-written biopsy explanations, all five were comfortable sharing only 40% of the reports, and at least one flagged severe harm concern in 20%. These findings suggest that patients may be protected when a clinician checks content before release.

commentary.research_gap: No trial randomizes clinical documents to clinician review versus no review and measures downstream patient harm. Studies have not measured how review accuracy changes with reviewer experience, fatigue, or document volume at scale. None tests aids that direct reviewer attention to likely errors, or audits that separate a signature from actual review.
commentary.underserved_note: Four tests included non-English documentation (Thai, Chinese, and European languages), and one included low-literacy patient leaflets. All five were offline or simulated. No test reported Medicaid or safety-net populations, and most real-deployment studies did not report patient demographics. The effectiveness and burden of review in these settings, where edit demands may be higher, remain untested.
